extracted.intended_audience: readers and researchers interested in Cornish folklore, local historians, and students of traditional drama
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative notes and commentary on Cornish miracle/Christmas plays, their characteristics, performance context, and historical value; useful for judging authenticity, entertainment quality, and preservation priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antiquity / origin
rubrics_metrics.description: These old plays are 'of very remote origin' and are 'founded probably on the old mysteries now reproduced in Yorkshire'—the plays' historical pedigree is a key attribute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess works for connections to ancient mystery-plays and their continuity with medieval religious drama; evidence of long-standing local tradition strengthens their historical value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Survival as literary remains
rubrics_metrics.description: Miracle plays represent 'almost the only remains of ancient Cornish literature' and thus their status as surviving texts/artifacts is an important criterion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value and prioritize texts/performances that preserve otherwise-lost local literary material; treat extant plays as important documentary evidence of regional culture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject-matter (religious/historical themes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical subjects include sacred or legendary topics (e.g., 'St. George and the Dragon', 'The Creation of the World', Noah's flood) often introduced or popularized by historical events like the Crusades.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or reconstructing a play, check that its subject aligns with known medieval religious/mystery themes; such alignment supports authenticity and contextual appropriateness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic/anachronistic elements and irreverence
rubrics_metrics.description: These plays frequently contain 'comic passages', 'ludicrous anachronisms', and scenes now possibly seen as 'irreverent, if not profane' (e.g., domestic squabbles in Noah's flood scene).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and preserve the bawdy or humorous elements and anachronisms as intrinsic features rather than defects; they reflect popular taste and performance conventions of the period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Popular entertainment value / audience delight
rubrics_metrics.description: Performances often prioritized audience amusement—episodes such as the prompter/actor exchange at St. Just provided 'much amusement'—so audience engagement is a criterion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate productions for their capacity to engage and amuse local audiences; spontaneous comic interactions and buffoonery were legitimate elements and indicators of success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance conventions and stock roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Plays used conventional roles and stage business (e.g., 'Mak, the buffoon', the ordinary/manager, prompter), and relied on familiar stage mechanics and improvisation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging or reconstructing performances, attend to established role-types and staging conventions; fidelity to these conventions supports historical plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Site and communal context (Plan-an-guary amphitheatres)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many ancient amphitheatres (the 'Round', Plan-an-guary, Redruth) are surviving venues tied to the plays; these public sites are integral to their social function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the original performance spaces and communal context in evaluations and restoration decisions; site preservation and community accessibility are important for authenticity and reuse ('these old Plan-an-guaries should be rebuilt and restored as public places of recreation, common to all').

rubrics_metrics.name: Regional linguistic and cultural resonance
rubrics_metrics.description: Local language and cultural references matter (the text notes the eastern lady thought 'our ancient language sounded much like her eastern tongue'), indicating cross-cultural echoes and local flavor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess texts/performances for dialectal features and local cultural markers; such features contribute to the work's identity and its interpretive value for folklorists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documentary anecdotes as interpretive evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Anecdotes, court records, and contemporary accounts (e.g., the Sanckras performance and subsequent brawl reported in a Hundred Court record) are used as evidence about play practice and reception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use archival anecdotes, legal records, and local testimony as legitimate sources for reconstructing performance circumstances and assessing historical authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restoration vs. fidelity tension
rubrics_metrics.description: While advocating restoration of physical sites, the author notes modern tastes ('We are become too fastidious and pious') may differ from historical norms, posing a tension between restoring form and preserving original spirit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When restoring or reintroducing miracle-plays, balance fidelity to historical content (including coarse or irreverent aspects) with contemporary sensibilities; document editorial choices and rationales.
